section.title: Life in the Spirit
section.sectionRationale: After the anguished cry of chapter seven, Paul steps into the sunlight of chapter eight, the mountaintop of the letter. He opens with the great verdict: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. What the law could not do, weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son as an offering for sin, condemning sin in the flesh. The Spirit of life now dwells in believers, raising them to walk a new way, and by that same Spirit of adoption they cry Abba, Father, as sons of God and heirs with Christ.
section.thesis: For those in Christ Jesus there is no condemnation, because God condemned sin in the flesh of His own Son; the indwelling Spirit gives life, leads them as sons of God, and by the Spirit of adoption they cry Abba, Father, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ.
section.frameNote: Five movements: no condemnation because God condemned sin in His Son; the mind of the flesh against the mind of the Spirit; the Spirit of life dwelling in and raising believers; sons of God led by the Spirit; and the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry Abba, making us heirs with Christ.

units.label: No condemnation in Christ Jesus
units.note: God condemned sin in the flesh of His own Son

verses.text: Therefore, there is now no {{katakrima|condemnation}} for those who are in Christ Jesus.
For in Christ Jesus the law of the {{pneuma|Spirit}} of life set you free from the law of sin and death.

For what the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the {{sarx|flesh}},
so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

units.label: The mind of the flesh and the mind of the Spirit
units.note: two ways of thinking, two destinies

verses.text: Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.
The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace,
because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God: It does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so.
Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God.

units.label: The Spirit of life dwelling in you
units.note: the same Spirit who raised Jesus

verses.text: You, however, are controlled not by the flesh, but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.
But if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, yet your spirit is alive because of righteousness.
And if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you.

units.label: Sons of God, led by the Spirit
units.note: an obligation not to the flesh

verses.text: Therefore, brothers, we have an obligation, but it is not to the flesh, to live according to it.
For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

units.label: The Spirit of adoption, heirs with Christ
units.note: by whom we cry Abba, Father

verses.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of {{huiothesia|adoption}} to sonship, by whom we cry, “{{Abba|Abba}}! Father!”
The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.
And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ; if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.

katakrima.gloss: Condemnation, the sentence of a judge against the guilty, the penalty pronounced and executed. Paul's opening word after chapter seven is that this sentence no longer stands over those in Christ Jesus. It is not merely that condemnation is postponed or reduced; there is now none at all, because it fell upon Christ in the sinner's place.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. In this passage it names the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of life, of God, of Christ, and of adoption. The Spirit is God Himself indwelling the believer, applying Christ's work, giving life to the dead, leading the sons of God, and witnessing that they belong to the Father.

sarx.gloss: Flesh. Paul uses it not merely for the physical body but for fallen human nature in its weakness and rebellion, the self turned away from God and unable to please Him. It is in the flesh, in the humanity of His own Son, that God condemned sin, so that those in Christ need no longer live under the flesh's rule.

huiothesia.gloss: Adoption to sonship, the legal act by which one who was not a child is given the full standing, name, and inheritance of a son. Believers do not receive a spirit of slavery and fear but the Spirit of adoption, placed as full sons in God's family with every right and hope that belongs to His own Son.

Abba.gloss: Abba, the Aramaic word for Father, the intimate address a child uses of a beloved father. It was the very word Jesus prayed in Gethsemane. By the Spirit of adoption the same cry rises from the hearts of believers, the assurance of a child who knows himself loved and secure in the Father's house.

basic.context: This is the summit of Romans. After the groan of chapter seven, where Paul cries out over his own inability to keep the law, chapter eight opens with relief and triumph. There is now no condemnation for those in Christ. God has done in His Son what the law could never do, and He has put His own Spirit within His people to give them life and lead them home as His sons.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this passage as the answer to chapters five through seven. The problem was condemnation and the power of sin; here is the verdict of no condemnation and the power of the indwelling Spirit. Notice the contrast that runs all through: flesh against Spirit, death against life, slavery against sonship. The passage moves from the courtroom, no condemnation, to the family, Abba, Father.
basic.originalLanguages: The opening word is katakrima, the judge's sentence of condemnation, now removed. The Spirit is the pneuma, God Himself indwelling the believer. Sarx, the flesh, is fallen human nature that cannot please God. Believers receive huiothesia, adoption to sonship, and by the Spirit cry Abba, the intimate Aramaic word for Father.
basic.typology: The sending of God's own Son as an offering for sin fulfills the whole sacrificial system, where a substitute bore the penalty of the guilty. The Spirit of adoption fulfills the promise that God would put His Spirit within His people and call them His sons, and the inheritance points beyond the land of Canaan to the whole redeemed creation shared with Christ.
basic.christ: There is no condemnation because God sent His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemned sin in Him. The Spirit who indwells is the Spirit of Christ. Believers are sons of God only because they are joined to the true Son, and they are heirs of God as fellow heirs with Christ, sharing His sufferings now and His glory to come.
basic.god: The Father is the one who acts throughout: He sends His Son, He condemns sin in the flesh, He gives His Spirit, He raises the dead, He adopts sons and makes them heirs. The passage shows the whole Trinity at work in salvation, the Father sending, the Son offered for sin, the Spirit giving life and crying Abba in our hearts.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 4 speaks of the Spirit of the Son crying Abba, Father, making us sons and heirs. Ezekiel 36 promises God will put His Spirit within His people. John 3 speaks of being born of the Spirit. Romans 5 declares peace with God and no more wrath for those justified by faith.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible moves from a garden lost to a family restored. Adam's race lay under condemnation and death; here God lifts the sentence in His Son and pours out His Spirit, turning slaves into sons who cry Abba, Father. The story runs on toward the inheritance, a redeemed creation shared with the risen Christ.

context.literary:
Chapter 8 opens with 'Therefore', and it takes the whole of the previous section's cry as its setting. The word 'now' in the first verse marks a change of time, from the 'wretched man' of 7:24 to the person who is declared free. The passage then falls into four movements. Verses 1 to 4 state the verdict and its ground. Verses 5 to 8 set out the two possible orientations of the mind. Verses 9 to 11 turn to the readers with 'You, however', and describe the Spirit's indwelling and its promise for the body. Verses 12 to 17 draw the practical conclusion, the debt, the Spirit's leading, and the family.

The vocabulary shows the turn. The Spirit, who is mentioned in 7:6 and then does not appear in the long struggle of 7:7 to 7:25, where the law is called 'spiritual' but the Spirit Himself is silent, appears again and again here. Paul uses a series of titles in verses 9 to 11, the Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus, and alongside them he says 'Christ is in you', so that the indwelling of the Spirit and the indwelling of Christ are spoken of together. The passage ends in the language of family, children, heirs, co-heirs, and with a condition about suffering that opens the way to the long reflection on suffering and hope in verses 18 to 39.

The shape is also one of reversal. In 7:23 Paul speaks of a 'law of sin' holding him captive. Here it is 'the law of the Spirit of life' that sets free. Condemnation, a word from the courtroom, is answered by sonship, a word from the home. The direction of the sentence moves from the verdict to the family and from 'no condemnation' in verse 1 to 'glorified with Him' in verse 17. The chapter as a whole is bracketed by two phrases, 'in Christ Jesus' in verse 1 and 'in Christ Jesus our Lord' in verse 39.
context.historical:
Paul wrote Romans from Corinth about the middle of the first century, and when he spoke of suffering with Christ in verse 17 he was writing to a church in the capital that would, within a decade, know what it was to suffer. The imperial city also gives the passage its pictures. Roman law knew adoption as a way of giving a person a new family in full. An adopted son took the new father's name, came under his authority and became his heir with all the rights of a natural child, and his old debts and ties fell away. The best known case in the first century was Octavian, made heir and son by the will of Julius Caesar, who went on to rule the empire as Augustus. When Paul spoke of adoption, which he does five times in his letters, Romans 8:15, 8:23, 9:4, Galatians 4:5 and Ephesians 1:5, his readers knew that it meant full standing in a household, with no second-class membership.

A Jewish reader would hear a second background. The adoption of a people had been Israel's privilege. 'Israel is My firstborn son,' God told Pharaoh, Exodus 4:22, and Paul lists adoption first among the gifts of Israel in Romans 9:4. One of the passage's wonders is that Gentile believers in Rome, with no such history, call out to God in an Aramaic word, Abba, that goes back to Jesus' own prayer, Mark 14:36. A Greek-speaking congregation was keeping a word from the speech of Jesus and Galilee on its tongue, and Galatians 4:6 shows it was a feature of churches beyond Rome too.

The mention of the Spirit would also have had weight. The prophets looked for a day when God would put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:27 and Joel 2:28, and Paul's readers, whether Jews who had waited for it or Gentiles who had been given it unexpectedly, were meant to see that what had been promised for the last days was now the ordinary possession of every believer.
context.canonical:
Romans 8:1-17 gathers threads from the whole Bible. The promise that God would put His Spirit within His people lies behind it. Ezekiel 36:26-27 speaks of a new heart, a new spirit and God's own Spirit within, causing His people to walk in His statutes, and Ezekiel 37:14 says, 'I will put My Spirit in you and you will live.' Jeremiah 31:33 says the law will be put in the mind and inscribed on the heart. Joel 2:28 says the Spirit will be poured out on all people.

The New Testament carries the same truth in several voices. Jesus told Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless born of water and the Spirit, John 3:5-8, and promised the disciples the Spirit who would be in them, John 14:16-17. Galatians 4:4-7 is the closest parallel to verses 14 to 17: God sent His Son to redeem those under the law that we might receive adoption, and sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father'. Galatians 5:16-25 sets out the contrast of flesh and Spirit in the form of a list of works and a list of fruit.

The sin offering of verse 3 draws on Leviticus, where the sin offering is the sacrifice that deals with guilt, and on the Servant of Isaiah 53:10 whose soul is made a guilt offering. Hebrews 10 reads the whole system as pointing to a body prepared for Christ. The word of 2 Corinthians 5:21, that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, is the closest New Testament summary.

The closing language of inheritance picks up Psalm 2:8, where the Son is told to ask for the nations as His inheritance, and Hebrews 1:2, where He is appointed heir of all things. First Peter 1:3-4 speaks of an inheritance that is imperishable and reserved in heaven, and Revelation 21:7 says that the one who overcomes will inherit all things and be God's son.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote this paragraph to remove a fear. After a chapter of honest struggle he knew that some of his readers would conclude that the Christian life is a permanent condition of being on trial. He answers that the trial is over. He wanted them to hear the verdict first, before any instruction, because every instruction in the passage depends on it. A person who thinks God is still deciding whether to condemn will obey from dread, and Paul says plainly that this is not the spirit that was given, verse 15.

He also meant them to understand that the verdict is not a legal trick. It rests on something God has done in the flesh of His Son, and it comes with a gift, the Spirit, who is the life of the person who has been acquitted. So the passage moves from the law court to the family, and its aim is to make the readers feel at home in the presence of God.

Finally, Paul wanted to give them a way to read their own lives. The tug of the flesh does not mean they have lost their standing, and the desire to please God is itself the work of the Spirit. The passage ends with an honest condition, suffering with Christ, because Paul does not want comfort to turn into ease. He gives them assurance and he gives them a road, and he wants them to see that the two belong together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the passage describes what is true of every believer: no condemnation, the Spirit's indwelling, a life that has a future, adoption and inheritance. The reader is not asked to produce any of these. They are stated as facts, introduced by 'if the Spirit of God lives in you', which is a way of saying that the Spirit's presence is what marks a Christian, not a second stage that some reach and others do not. Verse 9 puts it bluntly: anyone without the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him.

The prescriptions are few and come late. Verse 12 states that we have an obligation, and verse 13 says what it is, to put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit. Both come after the indicative. The order matters for application. Believers do not obey in order to reach the status of children; they obey because that is what children do and because the Spirit empowers it. Putting sin to death is a lifelong activity, in the present tense of the Greek, and it is carried out by the Spirit, not by the unaided will.

The last clause of verse 17 should be read with care. 'If indeed we suffer with Him' is not a condition for being a child, since the previous clauses have already said we are children, but the shape of the road to glory. It does not teach that all suffering is of this sort, or that Christians should seek suffering, only that those who belong to Christ will share in His path and His outcome.

debates.question: What does it mean that 'the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us', verse 4?

views.label: Christ's obedience counted as ours
views.case: Some, especially in the Reformation tradition, read the fulfilment as the law's demand being met on our behalf by Christ's obedience and death, which is counted as ours. The grammar supports it, since the verb is passive, 'be fulfilled', and the fulfilment is said to happen 'in us' and not 'by us', and the whole sentence is the purpose of God's sending His Son, verse 3.

views.label: Obedience produced by the Spirit
views.case: Others stress the second half of the verse, 'who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit'. On this view the law's requirement is fulfilled as the Spirit enables a life of love, which Paul says in 13:8-10 sums up the law. This fits Ezekiel 36:27, where the Spirit causes God's people to walk in His statutes.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many hold the two together. The verse speaks of a righteousness secured in Christ and then worked out in a Spirit-led life, so the passive verb and the walking clause are two aspects of the same gift. Neither is complete without the other, for Paul has taught in chapter 6 that those who are counted righteous also yield their members to righteousness.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that the law is not discarded but met. What the law could not produce in a sinner, God has done in His Son and carries on in His people by the Spirit, so the believer is neither left to earn what is required nor excused from living it.

debates.question: Is 'spirit' in verse 10 the human spirit or the Holy Spirit?

views.label: The human spirit, made alive
views.case: The sentence sets 'body' against 'spirit', and on this reading the believer's own spirit is alive because of righteousness. This matches the contrast Paul draws between the body that will die and the person already renewed within, as in 2 Corinthians 4:16.

views.label: The Holy Spirit, who is life
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the Greek can be read 'yet the Spirit is life', and since the whole passage speaks of the Spirit of God and of Christ, it would be natural for Paul to say the Spirit Himself is life because of righteousness. The next verse then follows, where the Spirit gives life to mortal bodies.

debates.bearing: In either case the sentence says that the body is under the sentence of death while the believer already has life, and that the life is secured by righteousness given in Christ, not earned. The disagreement does not alter the hope of verse 11.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by the flesh that cannot please God?

views.label: Fallen human nature in rebellion
views.case: The historic reading takes the flesh as sinful human nature turned from God, not the physical body as such; verse 7 says the mind of the flesh is hostile to God and cannot submit to His law, describing a spiritual condition, not mere bodily existence.

views.label: The physical body as inherently evil
views.case: Some have wrongly read the flesh as the body itself, treating matter as evil; this misreads Paul, who says the body will be given life by the Spirit and calls believers to present their bodies to God.

debates.bearing: The historic reading guards against despising the body and locates the problem in the heart's rebellion, which only the indwelling Spirit can overcome, so that the same body will one day be raised.

debates.question: Does putting to death the deeds of the body in verse 13 make our sonship depend on our effort?

views.label: The fruit and evidence of the Spirit's life
views.case: The Reformation reading holds that those who have the Spirit will, by that Spirit, put sin to death; the mortifying is the sure fruit of new life, not its price, for the passage grounds everything in there being no condemnation and in the free gift of adoption.

views.label: A condition we must meet to earn life
views.case: Some read it as a bare condition that leaves final salvation uncertain and resting on human performance.

debates.bearing: The gospel reading foregrounds grace: the Spirit given to sons enables and moves them to war against sin, so that their perseverance is the evidence of God's work in them, not the ground of their acceptance.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's first word of substance, katakrima, is a courtroom noun for the sentence that follows a guilty verdict, and he had used it twice in chapter 5, verses 16 and 18, for what Adam's trespass brought on all. The opening of chapter 8 is built to answer that: 'no condemnation, not one, now'. The Greek puts the negative first, ouden, 'nothing at all'. The related verb in verse 3, katekrinen, 'He condemned', belongs to the same family, and the point is that the sentence was carried out, not waived. Sin was condemned, and the condemnation fell where God chose to put it.

The BSB footnote at verse 1 records that some manuscript traditions add the words 'who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit'. The best-attested text ends the verse at 'Christ Jesus', and the clause belongs to verse 4. The footnote on verse 2 records another variation, 'me' for 'you', which shows how closely readers heard 7:24 and 8:2 together. The verb in verse 2, 'set free', is the same eleutheroo that was used for freedom from sin in 6:18 and 6:22, so the believer's liberation is spoken of in a single vocabulary across these chapters.

Verse 3 begins with a noun phrase that has no verb, to adunaton tou nomou, 'the impossible thing of the law', and states the reason, that the law was weakened by the flesh. Paul says the Son came 'in the likeness' of sinful flesh. The word homoioma, likeness, affirms that the Son's flesh was real flesh and yet marks a difference, since He is not sinful. The BSB footnote notes that the Greek reads 'in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin', and the phrase 'for sin', peri hamartias, is the ordinary expression the Greek Old Testament uses for a sin offering, as in Leviticus 4:3 and, quoted in Hebrews 10:6, Psalm 40. So the verse is saying that God sent His Son to be the sacrifice.

In verse 4 the 'righteous standard' is dikaioma, a singular noun, the requirement of the law taken as a whole. The verb 'be fulfilled' is a passive, plerothe, so the fulfilment is something that happens in us. Paul speaks of those who 'walk', peripateo, a Hebrew-flavoured word for the whole course of life, as in Ezekiel's promise that God would cause His people to 'walk in My statutes'.

The 'mind' of verses 5 to 7 is phronema, an orientation or set of the whole person, and the verb 'set their minds' is phroneo. It is not just thinking; it is what one's life is tuned to. The statement that the mind of the flesh is 'hostile to God', echthra eis theon, takes up the vocabulary of enmity from 5:10, where we were once enemies who were reconciled. The Spirit's mind is 'life and peace', the peace with God that 5:1 had said believers possess.

In verse 8 'cannot please' states an inability, and verse 9 qualifies by the Greek eiper, 'if indeed, since', a word that treats the Spirit's presence as a presumption of the sentence and not a doubt. 'Lives in you' translates oikei en humin, 'dwells in you', a word of residence, which echoes the picture of Ezekiel 37:14. The 'life' that God will give mortal bodies in verse 11 is the verb zoopoieo, which Paul also uses in 1 Corinthians 15:45 of Christ becoming a life-giving spirit.

Verse 13 contains two small points that carry weight. 'You will die' is the Greek mellete apothneskein, 'you are about to die', a statement of direction. And 'put to death' is a present tense, thanatoute, a continuing action. Verses 14 and 15 speak of being 'led', agontai, a passive, and of the Spirit of 'sonship', huiothesia, literally the placing of someone as a son, and Paul adds the cry krazo, a loud call, Abba ho pater, the Aramaic word followed by its Greek translation, as in Mark 14:36 and Galatians 4:6. Verse 16 shifts from huioi, sons, to tekna, children, the word for those born. Verse 17 is full of compounds, sunkleronomoi, co-heirs, sumpascho, suffer with, and sundoxazo, be glorified with, all pointing to a shared life with Christ.

typology.fulfillment: The sin offering of Leviticus 4 was the animal that carried the sin of an anointed priest or of the community, and its blood was brought before the LORD. When Paul says that God sent His Son 'as an offering for sin' he uses the Old Testament's technical expression, and Hebrews 10:5-10 says that the body prepared for Christ is the offering in which the whole system finds its end. The correspondence is exact in substance and surpassing in scale. It falls short only where the old sacrifices could not do the work, since the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sin, Hebrews 10:4, whereas the Son's single offering has condemned sin in the flesh once for all.

typology.type: The Spirit poured out, the dry bones alive
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones ends with the promise 'I will put My Spirit in you and you will live', Ezekiel 37:14, and the parallel promise of a new heart in 36:26-27. Paul's description of the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus giving life to mortal bodies, verse 11, is the first harvest of that promise. The vision was given to a nation in exile, and the fulfilment reaches to every believer in Christ. It falls short of the end only in this, that the Spirit's work has begun in the believer but the body still awaits its raising.

typology.type: Israel the son, brought out of Egypt
typology.fulfillment: God said of Israel, 'Out of Egypt I called My son', Hosea 11:1, and called the nation His firstborn, Exodus 4:22. The nation's sonship was real but corporate and often disappointing, a child that wandered. Jesus is the true Son who goes down into Egypt and comes out, Matthew 2:15, and whose sonship was never in doubt, Mark 1:11. Believers now share in His sonship through adoption, Galatians 3:26. The type falls short because Israel's sonship could be forfeited through disobedience, while those in the Son have received a Spirit by whom they cry Abba, and nothing will separate them from the love of God, Romans 8:39.

The promise of a land was the inheritance of Israel, and Canaan was the place of rest, Deuteronomy 12:9-10. In Christ the inheritance widens. Psalm 2:8 promises the nations to the Son, Hebrews 1:2 calls Him heir of all things, and Romans 8:17 says believers are co-heirs with Him. First Peter 1:4 describes an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, and Revelation 21:7 that the one who overcomes will inherit all things. The land is a first instalment of the whole renewed creation. The type falls short because Canaan could be lost, as it was in the exile, while the inheritance in Christ is kept for those who are kept for it.

study.christ:
The passage is about what happened in Christ and what is given in Him. Everything in verse 1 turns on the location, 'in Christ Jesus', which Paul uses to mean union with the one who bore the sentence. The ground for 'no condemnation' is not that sin is overlooked but that it has been dealt with, 'He thus condemned sin in the flesh', in the flesh of the Son. Condemnation did not vanish; it came to rest on Him. Isaiah had said the LORD would make the Servant's soul a guilt offering, Isaiah 53:10, and Paul says elsewhere that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Galatians 3:13 says He became a curse. Romans 8:34 puts the question again at the end of the chapter, 'Who is there to condemn us?', and answers with the one who died and was raised and is at the right hand of God.

The passage leads to Christ by His true humanity and sinlessness. He came 'in the likeness of sinful man', which means that He took our flesh, and Hebrews 4:15 adds that He was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. That is why His flesh could be the place where sin was condemned and not the place where it ruled.

It leads to Christ by the Spirit. Paul calls the indwelling presence 'the Spirit of Christ', and says that where Christ is in the believer the spirit is alive. The Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead is the guarantee that those who belong to Him will be raised, and Romans 1:4 says Christ Himself was declared the Son of God with power through the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection. First Corinthians 15:45 calls Him the life-giving Spirit. What the Spirit does in believers is to bring them into the life of the risen Lord.

It leads to Christ by sonship. The believer cries 'Abba' with the cry that Jesus Himself used in Gethsemane, Mark 14:36, in the same agony in which He prayed and obeyed. The Son by nature has opened the family to sons by adoption, Galatians 4:4-5, and John 20:17 shows Him telling Mary to go to His brothers and say that He is ascending to 'My Father and your Father'. Hebrews 2:10 says that God is bringing many sons to glory through the one who was made perfect through suffering. The believer is a co-heir, sharing the inheritance that Psalm 2:8 promises the Son and that Hebrews 1:2 says has been appointed to Him.

Finally it leads to Christ by suffering and glory. 'If indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him' sets the believer on the road the Lord took, Philippians 3:10 and 1 Peter 4:13. A caution applies. Not every detail of the passage is a picture of Christ, and Paul does not say that the Spirit is merely Christ under another name. The persons are distinguished throughout, the Father who sends, the Son who is sent and the Spirit who is given, and the unity of their work is what makes the passage so rich.
study.god:
This is the clearest picture of the Trinity in Romans, and Paul does not argue for it; he assumes it. The Father sends His Son, verse 3, condemns sin in the flesh, raises Jesus from the dead, verse 11, and adopts, verse 15. The Son is the one sent, in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering. The Spirit is called the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, indwells believers, gives life, leads, testifies and prompts the cry of Abba. Each person has a part, and none is merely a helper to the others. Paul's wording, in which the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ and Christ in you are used of one indwelling, shows that the work of God in the believer is the work of the whole God.

The passage also shows a God who is both a judge and a father without letting either displace the other. His justice requires that sin be condemned, and it is, in the flesh of His Son. His love gives the Son, and the God who does not spare His own Son, Romans 8:32, is also the Father who gives the Spirit of adoption. Paul does not explain how a just God can declare the guilty free of condemnation except by saying what God has done. The cross is where holiness and mercy meet, and the family is what grows from it.

He is a God who takes the initiative at every step. The believer is 'led', the Spirit 'testifies', adoption is received. In the whole passage the human beings are recipients and the grammar is passive. God does not wait for a person to make himself fit for adoption; He sends, condemns, raises and adopts. That does not make the believer passive in the Christian life, since the Spirit-led put sin to death, but it does mean that every activity rests on a prior act of God.

He is also a God who draws near. The Spirit lives in His people, and the phrase 'Abba' shows that the distance of the slave has become the nearness of the child. The same God who is holy and before whom the flesh cannot stand has made His home in them. That nearness is not a reduction of His majesty, for the Father who is addressed with such tenderness is the Father who raised Jesus from the dead. Yet it is a nearness of a kind that no fear can survive, as the first words of the paragraph say.

For worship, the passage invites us to approach with confidence and without presumption. We pray as children, and the Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's, so that assurance has a divine author. We pray, too, as those who will die, sufferers who await the redemption of the body, and who receive in the Spirit the first part of what is promised.

crossReferences.note: The closest parallel to verses 14 to 17. God sends His Son, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, and then sends the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father'. Paul draws the conclusion that we are no longer slaves but sons and heirs, which is the argument of Romans 8:15-17 in a shorter form.

God promises to give a new heart and put His own Spirit within His people, causing them to walk in His statutes. Romans 8 is the announcement that this promise has been kept, and verse 4, with its 'walk' language, is the New Testament echo of the Ezekiel promise.

The vision of the valley of dry bones ends with the promise of God's Spirit and of life. Paul's statement that the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus will give life to mortal bodies, verse 11, takes the vision and ties it to the resurrection of Christ.

Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless born of water and the Spirit, and that flesh gives birth to flesh while the Spirit gives birth to spirit. The contrast between flesh and Spirit in Romans 8 is the same one, set out by Paul as the difference between two entire ways of existing.

God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, that in Him we might become the righteousness of God. It states in a single verse the exchange that Romans 8:3 describes with 'an offering for sin', so that what is condemned in Him is what is freed in us.

Paul had said that one trespass brought condemnation for all and one act of righteousness brought justification and life. The 'no condemnation' of 8:1 answers the condemnation of Adam's sin, and the reader hears the whole drama of Adam and Christ gathered into the first verse of the chapter.

The chapter returns to the courtroom at its close. If God is for us, who can be against us, and who will bring a charge against God's elect, since it is God who justifies. The assurance of verse 1 is answered at the end by the figure of Christ who died, was raised and intercedes.

Walk by the Spirit and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Paul gives the working detail of Romans 8:5-13, with the lists of the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit, and shows what it looks like to be led by the Spirit and not under the law.

Jesus prays in Gethsemane, 'Abba, Father, all things are possible for You.' This is the cry that believers are given to share, so that the prayer of the Son in His agony becomes the prayer of the adopted in their own.

We are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. John holds together the present fact of sonship and the future glory in the same pattern as Romans 8:16-17: a status already given and a likeness still to come.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opens with human beings made in God's image and set in His presence, and Genesis 3 closes with them driven out under sentence. Everything in the Bible's story is a response to that expulsion. Romans 8:1 reverses it in the first sentence. 'Condemnation', the word Paul used for what Adam's trespass brought on all, is struck from the record for those in Christ. The garden's closed door begins to open.

The Old Testament had hinted at the family at the heart of that reversal. God called Israel His son and sent Moses to Pharaoh with the demand to let My son go, Exodus 4:22-23. The prophets lamented a son who would not listen and looked for a day when God would give a new heart and put His Spirit inside His people. Ezekiel 36 and 37 are the supreme examples. What was promised for the last days, the indwelling of God's Spirit, arrives in Romans 8 as the everyday gift of every believer, and with it the family of God is enlarged beyond Israel to include Jews and Gentiles alike.

The cross is the hinge. The Son is sent in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemns sin there, so that the verdict of Genesis 3 and the long record of Israel's failure meet their resolution in a single act. After it, the Spirit is given, the Spirit of the Son, who makes believers sons.

The passage stands between the already and the not yet. Believers have the Spirit and a standing as sons, yet bodies still dead because of sin, and they suffer with Christ. Paul will carry the thought forward in verses 18 to 25, where the whole creation groans with them, and he calls the Spirit the firstfruits. The story is moving to its last chapters, in which the sons are revealed and the creation itself is set free, Romans 8:19-21.

In the new creation the adoption is complete. Revelation 21:7 says that the one who overcomes will inherit all things, and that God will be his God and he will be God's son. The Spirit's cry of Abba becomes the open face-to-face life of a family at home, where nothing is any longer under a curse, Revelation 22:3-4. The trial is over and the family sits down to the table, and that was in the verdict of the first verse of Romans 8.

quiz.q: Why is there no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus?

options.text: Because God condemned sin in the flesh of His own Son, sent as an offering for sin.
options.note: The sentence fell on Christ, so none remains for those united to Him.

options.text: Because believers now keep the law well enough to satisfy God.
options.note: The law was powerless to do this; the ground is Christ's work, not our law keeping.

options.text: Because God has simply decided to overlook sin.
options.note: Closer: God does not hold their sin against them, yet not by overlooking it; He condemned it in His Son as an offering for sin.

options.text: Because sin does not really matter to God.
options.note: Sin mattered so much that it cost the sending and offering of God's own Son.

quiz.q: What is the contrast Paul draws between the mind of the flesh and the mind of the Spirit?

options.text: The mind of the flesh is death and hostile to God; the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.
options.note: Verses 6 and 7 set death and hostility against life and peace.

options.text: The flesh is the body and the Spirit is the soul, both equally good.
options.note: Closer: there is a real contrast, but the flesh here is fallen nature in rebellion, not simply the body.

options.text: Both minds can please God in their own way.
options.note: Paul says those controlled by the flesh cannot please God.

options.text: There is no real difference between them.
options.note: Paul draws the sharpest possible difference, death against life.

quiz.q: What does it mean that believers received the Spirit of adoption?

options.text: They are given full standing as sons of God and cry Abba, Father, no longer slaves in fear.
options.note: Adoption places believers as full sons who address God as Father.

options.text: They are put on probation until they prove themselves worthy.
options.note: Closer: sonship is real and present, but it is a settled gift, not a probation; the Spirit witnesses they are God's children now.

options.text: They become sons by their own effort and obedience.
options.note: Sonship is received as a gift through the Spirit, not earned.

options.text: They remain slaves who must live in fear of God.
options.note: Paul explicitly says they did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns them to fear.

quiz.q: What inheritance belongs to the children of God?

options.text: They are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, sharing His sufferings now and His glory to come.
options.note: Verse 17 names them heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.

options.text: A guarantee of comfort and ease in this life.
options.note: Paul says they suffer with Christ now before being glorified with Him.

options.text: Only a share in the land of Israel.
options.note: Closer: the inheritance idea is right, but it widens to all that belongs to Christ, the heir of all things.

options.text: Nothing certain; the inheritance is only a hope that may fail.
options.note: The inheritance is secure, grounded in union with Christ and the witness of the Spirit.

quiz.q: Who lives in the believer according to this passage?

options.text: The Spirit of God, the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead.
options.note: Verses 9 to 11 name the indwelling Spirit of God and of Christ.

options.text: Only a vague religious feeling.
options.note: Paul speaks of the personal Spirit of God, not a mere feeling.

options.text: The law of Moses written on stone.
options.note: It is the Spirit, not the external law, who now indwells and gives life.

options.text: The believer's own improved willpower.
options.note: Closer: real change does happen, but the power for new life is the indwelling Spirit, not human willpower.

questions: Paul begins with there is now no condemnation. How would truly believing that verdict change the way you face your guilt and failures this week?
The mind of the flesh and the mind of the Spirit are set on different things. What are the things of the Spirit that God is calling you to set your mind on?
The same Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you. Where do you most need to know His life and power at work in your mortal body and daily struggle?
You have received the Spirit of adoption and may cry Abba, Father. How does knowing yourself as a beloved son rather than a fearful slave reshape your prayers?
Believers are heirs of God who suffer with Christ before being glorified with Him. How does the certainty of the inheritance help you endure present suffering?

translationNotes.note: Some later manuscripts add who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit to the end of verse 1, borrowing from verse 4; the earliest texts end simply with those who are in Christ Jesus, making the verdict unconditional.

In the likeness of sinful man renders a phrase literally in the likeness of sinful flesh; the word likeness guards that the Son truly shared our humanity yet was without sin. As an offering for sin can also be rendered to deal with sin, echoing the sin offering of the Old Testament.
Co-heirs with Christ renders a Greek term meaning fellow heirs together with Him. The clause that follows makes clear that glory comes by the path of suffering with Him.
